newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Primakov meet on NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Primakov meet on NATO expansion.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov held a key meeting with President Bill Clinton on Monday that will set the tone for a U.S.-Russian summit this week focusing on NATO expansion.

U.S. officials were reticent ahead of the mid-afternoon White House meeting, but said "a lot of work" needed to be done to reach an agreement to meet Moscow's strong objections to plans for the eastward enlargement of the Western alliance.

Primakov arrived in Washington two days ago and met U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Saturday and Defence Secretary William Cohen on Sunday. He had further meetings with Albright Sunday and Monday.

"I would describe the discussions over the weekend as intensive and cooperative and in some cases productive, but it's really hard to predict where we're going to end up," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.

At the March 20-21 summit in Helsinki, Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin will be seeking an accommodation over NATO's plan to announce at a July summit in Madrid which East European countries it will invite to apply for membership.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, which all once belonged to the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact in the communist era, are believed to be the leading candidates.

Yeltsin, in improving health after lengthy bouts with heart disease and pneumonia, insisted on Sunday that he would demand a legally binding treaty barring Western forces from ever deploying in eastern Europe.

Yeltsin's remarks conflicted with reports suggesting Moscow was dropping this demand. NATO is offering Russia a charter that would give it the right to close consultation on European security issues but no power to veto NATO plans.
"Obviously we have not reached an agreement on the NATO-Russia charter," Burns said. "There's a lot of work that needs to be done before we have a charter agreement, to say the least."

U.S. officials say there is an element of bargaining in the Russian position, with Moscow holding out for concessions in other fields in return for accepting a NATO expansion plan they know the alliance is determined to pursue.
"The Russians are going to soak this for everything they can, and we know that," one official said.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Washington understood the "context" of Yeltsin's statements -- an apparent reference to domestic pressures on him -- and wanted to "work quietly through differences" over NATO.

"We've seen nothing communicated to us either publicly or privately that would indicate an incapacity on the part of these two leaders and these two governments to bridge whatever differences exist" on the issue, he said.
Officials suggested that a key focus this week could be on related issues of nuclear and conventional arms control that the two sides have been grappling with.
As a "sweetener" for NATO expansion, the West is offering Russia changes to the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe pact that would block an arms buildup around Russia's borders.

Of even more concern to Washington is to try to break a deadlock over nuclear arms control. The 1993 START-2 strategic arms pact is stuck in the Russian Duma (parliament), many of whose deputies fear it could hurt Russian security.

U.S. officials have spoken of preparing for a possible START-3 accord that would go beyond the major missile cutbacks envisioned in START-2. But they say negotiations cannot start until the Duma ratifies the earlier treaty.

One carrot that the United States can offer Moscow is support for its membership in global economic groupings like the World Trade Organisation and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.
